claims.evidence: This cites a behavioral measurement about saccade timing.

claims.claim: Deep layer V4 neurons encode more information about the direction of planned eye movements than do superficial neurons.
claims.source: This proposed early role for deep layer neurons in supporting saccadic decisions is consistent with recent findings showing that deep layer V4 neurons encode more information about the direction of planned eye movements than do superficial neurons (Pettine et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This cites a recent finding that supports the proposed functional role.

claims.claim: Prior studies on border ownership only evaluated border ownership selectivity at the preferred orientation of each neuron.
claims.source: Prior studies on border ownership only evaluated border ownership selectivity at the preferred orientation of each neuron (Hesse and Tsao, 2016; Zhang and von der Heydt, 2010; Zhou et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This characterizes the approach of prior studies.

claims.claim: Functional clustering is a recurring theme in primate cortical visual areas.
claims.source: Functional clustering is a recurring theme in primate cortical visual areas (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical organization.

claims.claim: Functional clustering has been reported for several modalities in V4 including orientation, hue, direction of motion, spatial frequency, and curvature.
claims.source: and has been reported for several modalities in V4 including orientation, hue, direction of motion, spatial frequency, and recently curvature (Hu et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2018; Roe et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2020; Tanigawa et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This cites multiple studies showing clustering of different features in V4.

claims.claim: Border ownership preference is preserved across layers within a vertical penetration.
claims.source: We find here that border ownership preference is preserved across layers within a vertical penetration, indicating that this modality is also organized in a columnar fashion.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the clustering findings.

claims.claim: The border ownership of an edge is computed based on stimulus features falling outside the cRF.
claims.source: Importantly though, border ownership is of a fundamentally different nature than these other modalities: the border ownership of an edge is computed based on stimulus features falling outside the cRF.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual point about the nature of border ownership computation.

claims.claim: The columnar organization of border ownership indicates that there is a systematic asymmetric arrangement of the extraclassical contextual information.
claims.source: Combined with our finding that early border ownership signals are computed by deep layer neurons rather than being passed on from upstream areas, this columnar organization has important implications for the functional anatomy. It indicates that there is a systematic asymmetric arrangement of the extraclassical contextual information, which, as argued above, may be provided through horizontal fibers and corticocortical feedback.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the columnar organization finding.

claims.claim: The clustered architecture of preferred border ownership requires clusters of asymmetric contextual information in cortex, such that opposite polarities of contextual information occur in distinct and complementary clusters.
claims.source: The clustered architecture of preferred border ownership therefore requires clusters of asymmetric contextual information in cortex, such that opposite polarities of contextual information occur in distinct and complementary clusters.

results.result: Border ownership selectivity occurs first in deep layer units of V4, with statistically significant differences emerging at 58.8 ms in deep layers compared to 67.3 ms in granular and 85.8 ms in superficial layers. This early deep layer selectivity was confirmed using multiple analysis methods (BOI functions and border ownership reliability) and was robust to subsampling controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C40 provide converging quantitative evidence from multiple analytical approaches showing earlier border ownership selectivity in deep layers. The subsampling control (C36) rules out sample size confounds, and the statistical comparisons (C37-C39) demonstrate significant differences with appropriate confidence intervals and p-values. The finding is internally consistent across different metrics.

results.result: The earlier selectivity in deep layers is specific to border ownership and not a general property of deep layer responses. Control analyses showed that responses to small ring stimuli in the classical receptive field had shorter latencies in granular layers, and contrast polarity selectivity did not show earlier emergence in deep layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 provide critical control analyses demonstrating specificity. The finding that different stimulus properties show different laminar timing patterns (C44, C45) strongly supports that the early deep layer border ownership selectivity is not an artifact of the recording method or general deep layer properties. This strengthens the interpretation of the main finding.

results.result: The earliest border ownership signals in V4 are not simply inherited from upstream areas but are computed by neurons in deep layers.
results.evaluation: This interpretive claim (C5, C43) is well-supported by the timing data showing earlier selectivity in deep versus granular layers. Since feedforward input from V2 primarily targets the granular layer (C73), and granular layer responses to classical receptive field stimuli are fastest (C44, C74), the early deep layer border ownership selectivity cannot be explained by simple feedforward inheritance. The logic is sound and supported by the data.

results.result: Border ownership preference is organized in columnar clusters spanning cortical layers in V4. Units on the same penetration typically share the same preferred side of border ownership (74.4% for well-isolated units, p=0.017; 71.7% including multiunits, p=0.005), and this clustering extends across layers (81.1% for well-isolated units spanning layers, p=0.010).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 provide statistical evidence for clustering with appropriate randomization tests and significant p-values. The finding is replicated with different unit selection criteria (well-isolated vs. including multiunits) and different penetration subsets (all penetrations vs. those spanning layers). The consistency across analyses and the use of appropriate statistical controls support this conclusion.

results.result: Orientation preference in V4 is organized in columnar clusters that extend vertically across layers. For 9 out of 18 penetrations with orientation-selective units spanning all three layers, the aggregate preferred orientation was statistically significant (p<0.05), suggesting that orientation domains in V4 are columnar.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 provide quantitative evidence with appropriate statistical testing. The finding that 50% of penetrations (9/18 for well-isolated units, 17/34 including multiunits) show significant clustering is consistent with the known heterogeneity of V4 organization. The conclusion (C58) is appropriately cautious, stating the data 'suggest' columnar organization rather than definitively proving it.

results.result: Border ownership selectivity often occurs for a range of border orientations, with preferred sides systematically organized in visual space. While there is a mild bias toward border ownership selectivity at the preferred orientation (average distance 27.6°, p=0.018), 29.7% of units show selectivity to orthogonal edges, and for all such units (24/24 well-isolated), the preferred sides form spatially contiguous regions. About 18% of border ownership units have preferred regions spanning at least 120°.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C70 provide converging evidence about the relationship between orientation and border ownership. The statistical tests are appropriate (randomization tests), and the finding that all 24/24 units with orthogonal selectivity show spatial contiguity (C67) is particularly striking. The quantitative measurements of angular spans (C69-C70) are clearly defined. The conclusion that the relationship between orientation and border ownership is 'surprisingly subtle' (C64) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Border ownership signals computed in deep layers may be part of signals fed back to upstream cortical areas or the oculomotor system early after stimulus onset.
results.evaluation: This claim (C6) is explicitly speculative, using 'may be' language. While the timing data (C86) and anatomical knowledge about deep layer projections (C82-C84) are consistent with this possibility, no direct evidence is provided that these signals actually reach upstream areas or influence oculomotor behavior. This remains a plausible hypothesis requiring future testing.

results.result: The columnar organization of border ownership indicates systematic asymmetric arrangement of extraclassical contextual information, possibly provided through corticocortical feedback and horizontal connections. The clustered architecture requires that opposite polarities of contextual information occur in distinct complementary clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 present logical inferences from the columnar organization finding. The reasoning is sound: if border ownership is computed from extraclassical context and is organized in columns with opposite preferences, then the contextual inputs must also be systematically organized. However, C96's claim about the specific anatomical substrate (horizontal fibers and feedback) is more speculative, appropriately qualified with 'suggest' and 'possibly.' The logical inference is supported, but the mechanistic details remain uncertain.

results.result: The study recorded from 685 well-isolated units and 765 multiunit clusters across 88 penetrations (81 with interpretable CSD) in two macaque V4 using laminar probes positioned orthogonally to the cortical surface. Border ownership selectivity was found in 51.1% of well-isolated units, with high proportions in all laminar compartments. CSD analysis showed consistent sink-source patterns matching prior studies and histological validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C30 describe the dataset and basic methodological validation. The sample sizes are clearly stated, the orthogonality metric is quantified (C19), and the CSD patterns are validated against multiple prior studies (C26) including one with histological verification (C27). The proportion of border ownership-selective units (C28-C30) is consistent with prior literature. These methodological claims are well-documented and internally consistent.

results.result: The study used appropriate surgical procedures, recording equipment, and behavioral controls. Two male rhesus macaques with no prior experimental history were used, with all procedures approved by IACUC. A transparent artificial dura enabled orthogonal probe positioning, and eye position was monitored with trials aborted for fixation breaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C110 describe standard methodological procedures that are clearly documented. The ethical approvals are stated (C100), the surgical approach is detailed (C101-C102), and the behavioral controls are appropriate (C110). These are straightforward methodological descriptions that can be taken at face value.

results.result: Receptive field mapping used modified Gabors and rings presented at 50-60 ms intervals on a 25×25 dva grid. Border ownership stimuli consisted of isoluminant squares (12-20 dva) with 54% luminance contrast in four conditions (2 positions × 2 polarities), presented for 500 ms after 400 ms fixation, with typically 8-10 repetitions per condition. CSD was calculated as the second spatial derivative of stimulus-triggered LFP.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C127 provide detailed stimulus parameters and experimental design. The parameters are clearly specified and appropriate for the research questions. The border ownership stimulus design (C122-C123) follows established protocols from prior work (Zhou et al., 2000). The CSD calculation method (C114) is standard. These methodological details are well-documented.

results.result: Data analysis used SpyKING CIRCUS for spike sorting with manual curation. Well-isolated units were identified by refractory periods, and multiunits required 5:1 signal-to-noise ratio. Border ownership selectivity was assessed using permutation tests (10,000 shuffles) on the border ownership index with p<0.05 threshold (Bonferroni corrected). Multiple inclusion criteria ensured proper stimulus placement relative to receptive fields. Time course analyses used postsynaptic kernel convolution, and confidence intervals were computed using bootstrap methods (2000 iterations).
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C148 describe comprehensive and appropriate analytical methods. The spike sorting approach (C128-C130) uses established software with quality criteria. The statistical tests are appropriate: permutation tests for border ownership (C134), randomization tests for clustering (C142), and bootstrap methods for confidence intervals (C138). The inclusion criteria (C133) are rigorous and ensure data quality. The methods are reproducible and statistically sound.

results.result: Established anatomical knowledge indicates that feedforward inputs arrive primarily in the granular layer, while horizontal and corticocortical feedback connections predominantly target superficial and deep layers. The V2-to-V4 projection is the most important feedforward input and targets mostly layer 4. Deep layer neurons have unique anatomical properties including tall pyramidal cells with apical dendrites reaching layer 1 and receiving input from nearly all cortical layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C72-C73, C76-C79 cite well-established anatomical knowledge with appropriate references. These are not new findings but rather established facts used to interpret the current results. The citations are appropriate and the anatomical descriptions are consistent with the literature. These claims provide necessary context for interpreting the laminar timing results.

results.result: After border ownership selectivity is established (200-500 ms), the average border ownership index tends to be higher in deep layers (0.50±0.02) than granular (0.43±0.02) or superficial (0.45±0.03), but differences do not reach statistical significance. Border ownership reliability saturates around 0.85 in all compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 appropriately report non-significant trends with exact p-values (p=0.051 and p=0.22). The authors correctly do not overinterpret these trends. The saturation of BOR (C42) is a descriptive observation. This is appropriate statistical reporting of negative/null results.

results.result: Border ownership selectivity occurs early after onset of the stimulus-evoked response, with the difference between preferred and non-preferred sides first becoming significant at 56.5 ms after stimulus onset for all border ownership-selective units.
results.evaluation: Claim C31 provides a population-level timing measurement with appropriate statistical testing (sign rank test p<0.05 for ≥20 adjacent ms). This finding is consistent with prior work (Zhou et al., 2000) as noted in the claim. The timing measurement is clearly defined and statistically validated.

results.result: Spike latency for stimuli in the classical receptive field is shortest in the granular layer in V4, similar to findings in other macaque visual cortical areas (V1, MT), though this may not be universal (e.g., anesthetized V2 shows longer layer 4 latencies).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 appropriately contextualize the current findings within the broader literature. The comparison to other areas (C74) is supported by citations, and the caveat about V2 (C75) shows appropriate nuance. This demonstrates that the control finding (C44) is consistent with expected laminar organization in V4.

results.result: Border ownership computation requires integration over large areas of visual space (from V2 studies). Border ownership signals are established in deep layers before 100 ms, fast enough for saccade planning within typical intersaccadic intervals (200-300 ms). Deep layer V4 neurons project to V2 (75% of feedback neurons) and superior colliculus, and encode information about planned eye movements, consistent with a role in oculomotor guidance.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C88 integrate the current timing findings with anatomical and functional knowledge from the literature. The timing argument (C86-C87) is logical: signals at <100 ms can influence saccades given 200-300 ms intersaccadic intervals. The anatomical projections (C82-C84) and functional properties (C88) are cited from the literature. This provides a coherent functional interpretation, though the causal role in saccade guidance remains to be directly tested.
